english_translation: The Matobo Hills have caves with rock paintings drawn long ago.

dialogue.shona: Makomo ekumatobo ane mapako ane mifananidzo yakatarwa kare kare.
dialogue.english: The Matobo Hills have caves with rock paintings drawn long ago.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Makomo [mountains] • ekumatobo [ekumatobo] • ane [ane] • mapako [plural pako] • ane [ane] • mifananidzo [mifananidzo] • yakatarwa [it (past) tarwa] • kare [kare] • kare [kare]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakatarwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakatarwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('mapako')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'mapako' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).

grammar_notes.title: Expressing 'Has/Have' and 'There Is/Are' ('-ne' & 'pane / kune')
grammar_notes.content: Shona does not use a separate verb like 'have'; instead, it combines a subject prefix with '-ne' ('with'). For people: 'ndine' (I have), 'une' (you have), 'ane' (he/she has), 'tine' (we have), 'vane' (they have). For things, the prefix matches the object: 'imba ine...' ('the house has...'), 'rori rine...' ('the truck has...'). When combined with the location prefixes 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-', it means 'there is / there are': 'pane' ('there is right here'), 'kune' ('there is in that area'), and 'mune' ('there is inside').
grammar_notes.rule: Person/Thing + -ne = has/have (tine = we have, ine = it has) | pane / kune / mune = there is / there are

cultural_notes.title: Ancient San Rock Art in the Caves of the Matobo Hills ('Makomo eMatobo')
cultural_notes.content: A UNESCO World Heritage Site south of Bulawayo, the Matobo Hills ('Makomo eMatobo') feature dramatic balancing granite boulders and hundreds of rock shelters ('mapako') adorned with sacred paintings ('mifananidzo yakatarwa kare kare') created by San hunter-gatherers thousands of years ago.

active_exercises.prompt: Complete this future weather forecast: 'Mangwana zuva ______ zvakanaka.' (Tomorrow the sun will shine brightly.)
active_exercises.explanation: 'Zuva' (sun) takes the prefix 'ri-' + future marker '-cha-' + '-buda' (come out/shine) -> 'richabuda'.

active_exercises.prompt: If a farmer says 'Gore rino takawana goho guru pamunda pedu', what happened?
options: They are waiting for the rain to start next month
They obtained a big harvest from their field this year
The river flooded and washed away the bridge
A strong wind blew from the east all afternoon
active_exercises.correct_answer: They obtained a big harvest from their field this year
active_exercises.explanation: 'Takawana' = 'we obtained/got', 'goho guru' = 'a big harvest', 'pamunda pedu' = 'from our field'.

active_exercises.prompt: You want to politely ask an elder or a group of guests to sit down ('gara'). Which imperative form should you use?
active_exercises.explanation: Adding '-i' to the verb stem ('gara' -> 'garai') forms the plural and polite command in Shona.
